title: Simulate CommonJS Module Cache & require()
subtopicTitle: Module Systems: ESM vs CommonJS & Circular Dependencies
problemStatement: Implement `createModuleEnvironment()` that exposes `defineModule(id, fn)` and `require(id)`. Modules must only be evaluated once; subsequent `require` calls must return the cached `module.exports` object.
interviewTrap: Forgetting to populate cache.set(id, mod) BEFORE calling the module factory causes infinite recursion on circular dependencies.

testCases.name: Exports and requires a module successfully
testCases.testFn: const env = createModuleEnvironment(); env.defineModule('math', (exports) => { exports.add = (a, b) => a + b; }); return env.require('math').add(2, 3);

testCases.name: Subsequent requires return cached instance without re-evaluating
testCases.input: verify factory is only invoked once
testCases.testFn: const env = createModuleEnvironment(); let calls = 0; env.defineModule('counter', (exports) => { calls++; exports.val = 42; }); env.require('counter'); env.require('counter'); return calls;

testCases.name: Throws descriptive error on unknown module ID
testCases.testFn: const env = createModuleEnvironment(); try { env.require('unknown'); return 'no-error'; } catch (e) { return e.message; }

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: CommonJS exports are evaluated at runtime and copied by value into a module.exports object. ESM exports are live references bound during static analysis, meaning changes in the exporter reflect immediately in the importer.
stepByStepWalkthrough: 1. Initialize execution context and environment records for CommonJS module.exports & require cache mechanics.
2. Execute logic adhering to ECMAScript standard specification.
3. Verify invariant boundaries and edge conditions.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In JavaScript engines (e.g. V8), CommonJS module.exports & require cache mechanics is optimized via inline caches, heap contexts, and bytecode translation.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does require() caching work in CommonJS?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: When `require(path)` is called: 1) Resolves absolute file path. 2) Checks `require.cache[resolvedPath]`. If present, returns `require.cache[resolvedPath].exports` immediately. 3) If not present, creates a fresh module object `{ id: resolvedPath, exports: {}, loaded: false }`, executes the module code inside a wrapper function, marks `loaded = true`, and returns `module.exports`.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is the CommonJS module wrapper function?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Node.js wraps every CJS file in an invisible IIFE before execution: `(function(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) { ... });`. This is why variables declared at the top of a file are NOT global, and why `__dirname` is available.

realWorldUseCases.description: Database connection clients export a single instantiated client: `require('./db')` returns the exact same cached instance across all controllers.

howToExplain.opening: CommonJS uses a synchronous module loader with an in-memory require.cache map, ensuring each module executes only once and shares its exports as singletons.
keyPoints: require.cache stores evaluated modules by resolved absolute path.
Subsequent requires return the cached exports object in O(1) time.
Modules are wrapped in an invisible function providing exports, require, module.
Deleting require.cache[path] forces re-execution on next require.
howToExplain.closingImpression: CommonJS module caching provides effortless singleton patterns across large Node.js architectures.
analogies: A library lending desk: the first person to ask for a book triggers the librarian buying it; everyone else borrows the same book from the shelf.

commonMistakes.why: exports is just a variable pointing to module.exports. Reassigning exports breaks the reference, leaving module.exports empty.

followUpDeepDive.question: How do you hot-reload a CommonJS module in development?
followUpDeepDive.answer: By deleting its entry from the cache: `delete require.cache[require.resolve('./module')]` and calling `require('./module')` again.
